title: Chapter II — The Locale of Savoy as a Field for Educational Enterprise
text:
Chapter II

The Locale of Savoy as a Field for
Educational Enterprise

Savoy Male and Female College owed its unusual growth to a combination of favorable factors, not the least of which was the nature of the locale in which it took root. Hardy pioneers had fought back the Indians a generation before the College was founded and devastating set-back of the Civil War had been overcome; and the section, a rich agricultural area, had entered upon a quarter century of economic progress and increase in population. The character of the population, too, was an important factor in the school's growth, for they who had been accustomed in an appreciation of culture and a demand for education.

ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF FANNIN COUNTY

FANNIN COUNTY DEED RECORDS. The Bonham News-Annual of 1884 gives the following list of pioneer history of the County of Fannin:

"Among the pioneers of Fannin County who drove back the bands of prowling Indians and opened up the way for civilization were Judge Bailey Ingish and his family, John L. German, John Thomas Ashcraft, and many other well-known, brave settlers. In 1836, R. H. Leeks, Thos. Journey, Jacob Black, Daniel Kitchens, Samuel Ligons, Isaac Newton, Thomas Ligons, James S. Baker, the Hunters, the Savoys, the Cox family, and Thomas E. Hooper and others who settled near the present site of Bonham. These are by no means all, as we have a reverence for these noble men who wore them [?] for their kindness, endurance, and bravery—armed with stout hearts and buried beneath the sod of the land they so bravely defended."
notes: First page of Chapter II. Printed page number 4 at bottom. Bonham News-Annual of 1884 quoted. The word 'them' marked [?] as uncertain reading.
